title: Acute Decompensated Heart Failure
profile: 68-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 25%), admitted to the cardiac step-down unit.

Notes: Client sitting upright on the edge of the bed, breathing fast and using accessory muscles. Productive cough with pink, frothy sputum. Crackles throughout both lower and middle lung fields. +3 pitting edema in both lower extremities. States, "I can't catch my breath."
Vitals: BP 188/104 mm Hg · HR 118 (sinus tachycardia) · RR 32 · SpO₂ 84% on 2 L nasal cannula · T 37.0 °C (98.6 °F)
BP 142/86 · HR 92 · RR 20 · SpO₂ 94% on 2 L
Labs: BNP 1,840 pg/mL (normal < 100) · Troponin I 0.02 ng/mL (normal < 0.04) · K⁺ 4.1 mEq/L · Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL · Na⁺ 136 mEq/L
Orders: Furosemide 40 mg IV push now · Oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥ 92%; BiPAP per respiratory therapy if SpO₂ < 90% · Nitroglycerin IV infusion, titrate per protocol for SBP > 140 · Strict intake and output · Daily weight · 2 g sodium, 1.5 L fluid-restricted diet

items.stem: Which findings require immediate follow-up by the nurse? Select all that apply.
options: Crackles in the lower and middle lung fields
items.rationale: Pink frothy sputum, crackles rising to the middle lung fields, hypoxemia and tachypnea show fluid filling the alveoli. Severe hypertension raises afterload and drives this "flash" pulmonary edema, so it also needs treatment now. The temperature, troponin and potassium are within normal limits.

items.stem: What is causing the client's pink, frothy sputum and low oxygen saturation?
options: High left ventricular filling pressure pushing fluid into the alveoli
Bacterial pneumonia filling the alveoli with pus
A new myocardial infarction damaging the left ventricle
A pulmonary embolism blocking blood flow to the lungs
items.rationale: A failing left ventricle cannot empty. Pressure backs up into the pulmonary capillaries until fluid and red cells leak into the alveoli, which causes the pink froth and blocks oxygen exchange. No fever points away from pneumonia, a normal troponin argues against a new MI, and crackles with frothy sputum do not fit a PE.

items.stem: The client is at highest risk for which life-threatening complication?
options: Acute respiratory failure from cardiogenic pulmonary edema
items.rationale: With an SpO₂ of 84% on oxygen, a respiratory rate of 32 and accessory muscle use, the client is close to respiratory failure. Hypokalemia and kidney injury are later risks of treatment. DVT is not the immediate threat.

items.stem: For each intervention, mark whether it is indicated, non-essential, or contraindicated right now.
rows: Move to BiPAP or high-flow oxygen
Give a 500 mL 0.9% sodium chloride bolus
Lay the client flat with legs elevated
Weigh the client on a standing scale now
items.rationale: Diuresis and better oxygen support treat the cause and the hypoxemia. A fluid bolus adds volume to lungs that are already flooded. Lying flat with legs up increases venous return and worsens the edema. Daily weight matters for tracking, but standing a hypoxic client on a scale now is unsafe and can wait.

items.stem: Which action should the nurse take first, before giving the IV furosemide?
options: Raise the head of the bed to high-Fowler's with legs dependent and increase oxygen support
Give the furosemide immediately, then reposition
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to measure output
items.rationale: Airway and breathing come first. Sitting upright with the legs down reduces venous return and lets the diaphragm move, and stepping up oxygen (non-rebreather or BiPAP per order) treats the hypoxemia. These take seconds, and then the diuretic is given. A catheter and repeat labs can follow.

items.stem: At 07:30, after 1,200 mL of urine output: for each finding, mark whether the client has improved, not changed, or declined.
rows: Crackles now only at the bases
items.rationale: Breathing, oxygenation, lung sounds and blood pressure show a good response. Peripheral edema clears more slowly than lung fluid. The new low potassium is a common side effect of loop diuretics and raises the risk of dysrhythmias, so report it and expect replacement.

title: Septic Shock from Urosepsis
profile: 74-year-old woman sent from a skilled nursing facility with an indwelling urinary catheter and new confusion.

Notes: Client lethargic and responds only to painful stimuli (baseline: alert, oriented to person and place). Urine in the drainage bag is dark amber and cloudy with heavy sediment. Skin warm and flushed. Capillary refill 4 seconds.
Vitals: BP 78/42 mm Hg (MAP 54) · HR 126 · RR 26 · T 39.2 °C (102.6 °F) · SpO₂ 93% on room air · Weight 60 kg
Labs: WBC 19,800/µL with 18% bands · Lactate 4.2 mmol/L (normal < 2.0) · Glucose 148 mg/dL · Platelets 110,000/µL · Creatinine 1.9 mg/dL (baseline 1.0)
Orders: Blood cultures × 2 · Urine culture from a newly placed catheter · Lactated Ringer's 30 mL/kg IV (1,800 mL) · Piperacillin-tazobactam IV · Norepinephrine infusion, titrate to MAP ≥ 65 mm Hg · Repeat lactate in 2 hours · Replace the indwelling urinary catheter

items.stem: Tap the findings in the record that show poor blood flow to the tissues (hypoperfusion).
items.rationale: A MAP below 65, a lactate above 2 (here 4.2), slow capillary refill and a drop in consciousness all show that organs are not getting enough oxygen. Fever, cloudy urine and flushed skin point to infection and vasodilation but do not by themselves measure perfusion. Mild hyperglycemia is a stress response.

items.stem: Which mechanism is mainly causing the client's low blood pressure?
options: Bacterial toxins causing widespread vasodilation and leaky capillaries
Pump failure from a weakened left ventricle
Low blood sugar reducing vascular tone
items.rationale: Septic shock is distributive shock. Inflammatory mediators triggered by the infection dilate blood vessels and make capillaries leak, so blood pools and fluid shifts out of the vessels. Nothing suggests bleeding or heart failure, and the glucose is high, not low.

items.stem: Which problem needs immediate resuscitation?
items.rationale: Hypotension (MAP 54), a lactate of 4.2 and new organ dysfunction (confusion, creatinine nearly double baseline) show sepsis with hypoperfusion that is progressing to septic shock, which carries the highest risk of death. Confusion here comes from poor brain perfusion, not from a new environment.

items.stem: The 30 mL/kg lactated Ringer's bolus has been started. Put the remaining hour-1 actions in order. Tap each in sequence; tap again to undo.
steps: Give the first dose of broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
Start norepinephrine if MAP stays below 65 mm Hg after the bolus
items.rationale: The Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle: measure lactate (already done), start 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 (running now), draw blood cultures before antibiotics so the organism can still be identified, give broad-spectrum antibiotics without delay, and add a vasopressor if MAP stays under 65 after the fluid challenge.

items.stem: The ordered 30 mL/kg (1,800 mL) of lactated Ringer's has infused. BP is now 82/46 mm Hg (MAP 58). Which action is the priority?
options: Start and titrate the norepinephrine infusion to keep MAP ≥ 65 mm Hg
Give another 2 L fluid bolus before starting a vasopressor
Place the client flat with legs raised and recheck in 30 minutes
Give acetaminophen to lower the fever, then reassess
items.rationale: The client has had the full fluid challenge and is still hypotensive, which is septic shock that needs a vasopressor. Norepinephrine is first-line; it is given through a central line when possible (a large, well-placed peripheral IV is acceptable for a short time, checked often for extravasation). More fluid without reassessment risks fluid overload, and waiting delays perfusion.

items.stem: Four hours after resuscitation: for each finding, mark whether the client has improved, not changed, or declined.
items.rationale: Lactate clearance, urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/h, a MAP at goal and better responsiveness show that tissue perfusion is improving. Falling platelets can signal developing coagulopathy (DIC), so report them. White cells take days to fall once antibiotics start.

title: Acute Compartment Syndrome
sub: After tibial fracture surgery · Orthopedic unit
profile: 24-year-old man, 14 hours after open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of a closed right tibial shaft fracture.

Notes: Reports right lower leg pain rising to 10/10, not relieved by IV morphine 4 mg given 30 minutes ago. Right calf tense, firm ("wood-like") and shiny. Passively flexing the right great toe upward causes severe pain. Surgical dressing feels tight.
Vitals: BP 142/88 mm Hg · HR 102 · RR 20 · SpO₂ 98% on room air · T 37.2 °C (99 °F)
Right dorsalis pedis pulse +1 (left +2) · Right foot warm · Light touch intact; tingling between the first and second toes · Capillary refill 3 seconds
Labs: Hgb 12.8 g/dL · K⁺ 4.4 mEq/L · Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · CK 1,150 U/L (expected after surgery)
Orders: Morphine 4 mg IV every 2 hours as needed for pain · Neurovascular checks every hour · Elevate right leg on pillows · Ice to the right leg as needed · Notify orthopedic surgery of neurovascular changes

items.stem: Which findings are early warning signs of rising pressure in the muscle compartment? Select all that apply.
options: Severe pain when the toe is passively stretched
Tingling between the first and second toes
Right dorsalis pedis pulse palpable at +1
items.rationale: Pain out of proportion to the injury, pain on passive stretch, a tense compartment and new paresthesia are the earliest signs. The deep peroneal nerve supplies the first web space, so tingling there is an early nerve warning. A warm foot and a palpable pulse are often still present early and do not rule it out; a pulse weaker than the other side (+1 vs. +2) is a late sign. Report it, but it is not an early warning. A mildly raised CK is expected after bone surgery.

items.stem: The client's right dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable at +1. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: It does not rule out compartment syndrome; pulses often remain until very late
It rules out compartment syndrome because arterial flow is present
It shows the pain is from the surgical incision
It means the pain medicine dose is too low
items.rationale: Compartment pressure first collapses the low-pressure veins and capillaries. Arterial pulses can stay palpable until muscle and nerve damage is already severe. Waiting for a lost pulse means waiting too long.

items.stem: These findings represent which urgent priority?
options: Impending muscle and nerve death from high compartment pressure
Deep vein thrombosis of the right calf
items.rationale: Within 4 to 6 hours, ischemia from high compartment pressure can cause permanent muscle and nerve damage, contracture or limb loss, and can trigger rhabdomyolysis. DVT does not cause pain on passive toe stretch with paresthesia. Fat embolism presents with breathing problems, confusion and petechiae. Infection usually appears later.

items.stem: For each intervention, mark whether it is indicated or contraindicated now.
rows: Keep the right leg elevated above the level of the heart
Loosen the tight dressing (and ask the surgeon about splitting any cast)
Apply ice packs to the calf
Keep the client NPO (nothing by mouth) for possible surgery
Give more morphine and reassess the leg in 1 hour
items.rationale: Raising the leg above the heart lowers arterial pressure into a compartment that is already squeezed, and ice constricts vessels. Both reduce blood flow and should be stopped even though they were ordered after surgery. Release anything tight, call the surgeon now, and keep the client NPO for an emergency fasciotomy. Medicating and waiting delays a time-critical diagnosis.

items.stem: While waiting for the orthopedic surgeon to arrive, how should the nurse position the right leg?
options: Elevated on two pillows above the heart
Lowered below the level of the bed
items.rationale: Keeping the limb level with the heart balances venous drainage against arterial inflow, which gives the best blood flow to the compartment. Elevation reduces arterial inflow; lowering the leg increases swelling.

items.stem: Twelve hours after an emergency fasciotomy: for each finding, mark whether the client has improved, not changed, or declined.
rows: Tingling between the toes has resolved
items.rationale: Returning sensation, soft compartments, controlled pain and a stronger pulse confirm the decompression worked. Tea-colored urine with a very high CK signals rhabdomyolysis from damaged muscle. Report it and expect aggressive IV fluids and close monitoring of kidney function and potassium.

title: Sepsis After Surgery
sub: Post-op day 2, sigmoid colectomy · Surgical unit
profile: 72-year-old client on post-op day 2 after a sigmoid colectomy.

Notes: New confusion: oriented to self only (yesterday oriented × 4). Skin warm, flushed. Reports abdominal pain 3/10. Incision edges approximated, no drainage.
Vitals: T 38.9 °C (102 °F) · HR 118 · RR 24 · BP 88/50 (MAP 63) · SpO₂ 93% on room air · Weight 70 kg
Labs: WBC 17.8 × 10³/µL · Lactate 4.1 mmol/L · Na⁺ 139 mEq/L · Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL (baseline 0.9) · Hgb 11.9 g/dL
Orders: Urine output 90 mL over the last 6 hours

Notify provider for SBP < 90, HR > 110 or new confusion · Sepsis protocol: if screen positive, the nurse may draw blood cultures × 2 and a lactate and start lactated Ringer's 30 mL/kg IV while notifying the provider

items.stem: Select all findings that require immediate follow-up.
items.rationale: Fever, tachycardia, hypotension, lactate ≥ 4, acute confusion and oliguria (< 0.5 mL/kg/h) are signs of sepsis with hypoperfusion. Pain 3/10 and a normal sodium are expected.

items.stem: Complete the sentence.

blanks.pre: The client's findings are most consistent with

items.rationale: Lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L or hypotension define sepsis with hypoperfusion and trigger the full fluid bolus. Creatinine near double baseline with oliguria points to AKI from poor perfusion. Anastomotic leak is a likely source after colectomy.

items.stem: Which condition is the client at highest immediate risk of developing?
items.rationale: Persistent hypotension needing vasopressors after fluids defines septic shock, with the highest short-term mortality. The others are real post-op risks but not the most immediate threat.

items.stem: For each potential order, mark whether it is indicated or not indicated.
rows: Furosemide 40 mg IV for low urine output
Hold IV fluids because of the client's age
items.rationale: These follow the Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle. Diuretics in a hypoperfused client worsen the kidney injury. Age alone is not a reason to withhold resuscitation, though lungs are reassessed after each bolus.

items.stem: Select all actions the nurse should take now.
options: Call the provider using SBAR and request a sepsis evaluation / rapid response
Draw blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose
Increase vital signs to at least every 15 minutes
Encourage the client to ambulate to raise BP
Give acetaminophen and recheck vitals in 4 hours before calling
items.rationale: Escalate now, follow the bundle order (cultures, then antibiotics), resuscitate, and watch closely. Ambulating a hypotensive, confused client risks a fall; treating the fever and waiting delays sepsis care.

items.stem: Three hours later: for each finding, mark whether the client's condition has improved, not changed, or declined.
items.rationale: Perfusion markers are improving. New crackles with falling SpO₂ suggest fluid overload: report it, slow fluids per order, and expect vasopressors if MAP falls. Mental status has not yet improved.

title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
profile: 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, brought to the emergency department after 2 days of vomiting. She ran out of insulin 3 days ago.

Notes: Drowsy but opens eyes to voice and answers questions slowly. Deep, rapid breathing with a fruity odor on the breath. Dry mucous membranes; skin tenting on the forearm. Reports abdominal pain 6/10 and constant thirst. Her mother says she has been urinating "all the time."
Vitals: BP 96/58 mm Hg · HR 124 (sinus tachycardia) · RR 30, deep · T 37.4 °C (99.3 °F) · SpO₂ 99% on room air · Weight 55 kg (121 lb)
Labs: Glucose 486 mg/dL (27 mmol/L) · Venous pH 7.14 · HCO₃⁻ 9 mEq/L · Anion gap 26 · Beta-hydroxybutyrate 6.2 mmol/L (normal < 0.6) · K⁺ 5.4 mEq/L · Na⁺ 131 mEq/L · Cl⁻ 96 mEq/L · BUN 32 mg/dL · Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL · Urine ketones large
Orders: 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L IV over 1 hour, then per DKA protocol · Regular insulin IV infusion 0.1 unit/kg/h (5.5 units/h); hold and notify provider if K⁺ < 3.5 mEq/L · Add potassium chloride to IV fluids per protocol when K⁺ < 5.0 mEq/L and urine output is adequate · Change to dextrose 5% in 0.45% sodium chloride when glucose < 250 mg/dL · Point-of-care glucose every hour · Basic metabolic panel, venous pH and beta-hydroxybutyrate every 2 hours · Continuous cardiac monitoring · Strict intake and output

items.stem: Tap the findings that show ketoacidosis, not just a high blood sugar.
items.rationale: Ketoacidosis means acid is building up. Kussmaul breathing, acetone (fruity) breath, a low pH, a low bicarbonate, a high anion gap and a high ketone level all show it. Thirst, frequent urination and a high glucose come from hyperglycemia alone and are also seen in hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, which has no major acidosis. A temperature of 37.4 °C is not a sign of ketoacidosis.

items.stem: Complete the sentences.

blanks.pre: The client's deep, rapid breathing is the body's attempt to
Although the serum potassium is 5.4 mEq/L, total body potassium is most likely

opts: acidosis and lack of insulin move potassium out of the cells while it is lost in the urine
the kidneys hold on to potassium during dehydration
blanks.answer: acidosis and lack of insulin move potassium out of the cells while it is lost in the urine

items.rationale: Ketones are acids, so this is a metabolic acidosis. The lungs compensate by breathing deep and fast to remove CO₂. Without insulin, and with acid in the blood, potassium moves out of the cells into the serum, so the lab value looks normal or high. Meanwhile osmotic diuresis and vomiting have drained the body's stores. The kidneys are losing potassium, not holding it, and nothing in the record suggests hemolysis.

items.stem: Once the insulin infusion is running, the client is at highest risk for which life-threatening complication?
options: Hyperkalemia from potassium added to the IV fluids
Fluid overload from the 0.9% sodium chloride
items.rationale: Insulin drives potassium back into the cells, and fluids dilute it, so serum potassium can drop fast in a client whose total stores are already low. Severe hypokalemia causes dysrhythmias and cardiac arrest. Potassium is added only when the level falls below 5.0 and urine output is adequate, which guards against hyperkalemia. A young adult with a large fluid deficit is at low risk for overload. Hypercalcemia is not a feature of DKA.

items.stem: At 10:00, for each order, mark whether it is indicated or not indicated now.
rows: 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L IV over the first hour
Regular insulin IV infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/h
Sodium bicarbonate IV to correct the pH of 7.14
Add 40 mEq potassium chloride to the first liter of fluid
items.rationale: Isotonic fluid comes first to restore volume and kidney blood flow. The insulin infusion can start because potassium is above 3.5 mEq/L. Bicarbonate is considered only when pH is below 7.0; fluids and insulin will correct this acidosis. Potassium is not added while it is 5.4 mEq/L, but it will be needed soon. Cardiac monitoring catches potassium-related rhythm changes, and hourly glucose guides the insulin and the switch to dextrose.

items.stem: At 14:00 the glucose is 244 mg/dL, pH 7.24, HCO₃⁻ 14 mEq/L, anion gap 18 and K⁺ 4.0 mEq/L. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Change the IV fluid to dextrose 5% in 0.45% sodium chloride with potassium and continue the insulin infusion
Stop the insulin infusion because the glucose is close to target
Give subcutaneous insulin and stop the IV insulin now
items.rationale: Glucose falls faster than ketones clear. Adding dextrose when glucose drops below 250 mg/dL lets the insulin keep running (the rate may be lowered per protocol) until the acidosis resolves, without causing hypoglycemia. Stopping insulin now would let ketones build up again. The switch to subcutaneous insulin waits until DKA has resolved and the client can eat, with the IV and subcutaneous doses overlapping by 1 to 2 hours. 50% dextrose is a treatment for hypoglycemia, which she does not have.

items.stem: Review the trend. For each finding at 18:00, mark whether the client has improved, not changed, or declined.
items.rationale: The pH, bicarbonate, anion gap and ketones are all moving toward normal, and her mental status and pain have improved. DKA is not resolved until ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L (with venous pH 7.3 or higher or bicarbonate 18 mEq/L or higher), so insulin is still needed. Potassium has dropped below 3.5 mEq/L because insulin keeps moving it into the cells. Follow the order: hold the insulin infusion, notify the provider and expect faster potassium replacement. Insulin restarts once potassium is back above 3.5 mEq/L, because ketones must still be cleared.

title: Postpartum Hemorrhage
sub: Uterine atony after vaginal birth · Labor and delivery
profile: 34-year-old, G4 P4, 45 minutes after the vaginal birth of a 4.3 kg (9 lb 8 oz) newborn after 22 hours of labor augmented with oxytocin. History of mild intermittent asthma.

Notes: Placenta delivered intact at 15:08. First-degree perineal laceration repaired. Peripad soaked in 10 minutes, with a steady trickle of bright red blood and clots. Fundus boggy, 2 cm above the umbilicus, midline. Client states, "I feel dizzy and cold." Skin pale and clammy.
Vitals: BP 96/58 mm Hg · HR 122 · RR 24 · SpO₂ 97% on room air · T 37.6 °C (99.7 °F)
Labs: Hgb 11.8 g/dL · Platelets 210,000/µL · Fibrinogen 420 mg/dL · Blood type O positive, antibody screen negative
Orders: Oxytocin 30 units in 500 mL lactated Ringer's IV; increase per postpartum hemorrhage protocol · Methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM per protocol · Carboprost 250 mcg IM per protocol · Misoprostol 800 mcg sublingual or rectal per protocol · Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes within 3 hours of birth · Type and crossmatch 2 units packed red blood cells · Quantitative blood loss (QBL) every 15 minutes

items.stem: Review the flow sheet. Which findings require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Boggy fundus 2 cm above the umbilicus
items.rationale: A boggy, high fundus and a pad soaked in minutes show active bleeding. Blood loss of 1,000 mL or more, a heart rate climbing every 15 minutes, a falling BP and dizziness with clammy skin show hypovolemia. A shock index (HR ÷ systolic BP) of 1.27 is well above the warning level of 0.9. A temperature up to 38 °C (100.4 °F) is common in the first 24 hours after birth, the SpO₂ is normal, and the admission platelet count is normal.

items.stem: What is the most likely cause of this client's bleeding?
options: An unrepaired vaginal or cervical laceration
items.rationale: Atony causes most postpartum hemorrhages. A soft, boggy uterus cannot squeeze the open blood vessels at the placental site closed. A large baby and a long labor with oxytocin both overstretch and tire the uterus. The placenta was delivered intact. Bleeding from a laceration continues while the fundus is firm. The platelet count and fibrinogen were normal.

items.stem: Complete the sentence.

blanks.pre: because her cumulative blood loss is
opts: 1,000 mL or more with signs of hypovolemia
unknown until the next hemoglobin result
blanks.answer: 1,000 mL or more with signs of hypovolemia

blanks.pre: and her most immediate risk is

items.rationale: Postpartum hemorrhage is cumulative blood loss of 1,000 mL or more, or any blood loss with signs of hypovolemia, within 24 hours of birth. Measured (quantitative) blood loss is used instead of a hemoglobin, which lags behind acute loss. Her BP is low, so this is not preeclampsia. With ongoing bleeding, the threat is hypovolemic shock. DVT and infection are later risks.

items.stem: The provider is on the way. For each medication in the hemorrhage protocol, mark whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this client.
rows: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes
items.rationale: Oxytocin is first-line. Methylergonovine is avoided in hypertension and preeclampsia, but her BP is low, so it is safe. Carboprost can cause severe bronchospasm and is contraindicated with asthma. Tranexamic acid is added to uterotonics once a hemorrhage is diagnosed and works only when given within 3 hours of birth; she is 45 minutes postpartum. Misoprostol has no contraindication here. Undiluted oxytocin given by fast IV push can cause sudden hypotension and dysrhythmias, so it is given as an infusion or IM.

items.stem: The provider has been paged. Select all actions the nurse should take now.
options: Massage the fundus firmly with one hand while the other hand supports the lower uterine segment
Call for help and activate the obstetric hemorrhage response
Increase the oxytocin infusion rate per protocol
Start a second large-bore IV (16–18 gauge) and send a type and crossmatch
Weigh all pads and underpads to update the QBL
Help the client walk to the bathroom to empty her bladder
Give oral fluids and reassess in 30 minutes
Put the newborn to breast instead of increasing the oxytocin
items.rationale: Fundal massage with lower-segment support firms the uterus without risking inversion. A hemorrhage needs more hands, uterotonics, IV access for fluids and blood, and accurate measurement (1 g of weight equals about 1 mL of blood). A dizzy, hypotensive client must not walk; if her bladder is full, catheterize her. Oral fluids may delay surgery and do not replace blood. Breastfeeding releases some oxytocin but is not a substitute for treatment during an active hemorrhage.

items.stem: Forty-five minutes after treatment: for each finding, mark whether the client has improved, not changed, or declined.
rows: Fundus firm, at the umbilicus, midline
Pad weights show 40 mL of blood loss over the last 30 minutes
Less dizzy; skin warm and dry
items.rationale: A firm fundus, small pad weights and better vital signs show the bleeding is controlled. Oxygenation was normal before and is still normal. The hemoglobin drop is expected after this much blood loss and often falls further as fluids are given. Report it so the provider can decide about transfusion and iron, and keep assessing the fundus and bleeding.

title: Severe Asthma Exacerbation
profile: 6-year-old boy (22 kg) with persistent asthma, brought by his father after 2 days of cold symptoms and 1 day of worsening cough and wheezing. He has used his albuterol inhaler 6 times since midnight.

Notes: Sitting upright and leaning forward on his arms. Speaks 2 to 3 words at a time. Suprasternal and intercostal retractions with nasal flaring. Inspiratory and expiratory wheezes in all fields; air movement diminished at the bases. Father says his daily inhaled corticosteroid "ran out last month."
Vitals: HR 148 · RR 44 · SpO₂ 89% on room air · BP 104/64 mm Hg · T 37.8 °C (100.0 °F)
Orders: Oxygen to keep SpO₂ 94–98% · Albuterol 2.5 mg with ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized every 20 minutes × 3 · Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO (13 mg) now · Magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg IV (1,100 mg) over 20 minutes if no improvement after the first hour · Continuous pulse oximetry and cardiorespiratory monitoring · Notify provider for SpO₂ < 90% on oxygen, decreasing breath sounds or change in mental status

items.stem: Tap the findings that show severe respiratory distress.
passage: Speaks 2 to 3 words at a time
Inhaled corticosteroid ran out last month
items.rationale: The tripod position, speaking only in short phrases, retractions, nasal flaring, a respiratory rate about twice normal for age (about 18 to 25) and an SpO₂ below 90% all mark a severe exacerbation. The BP is normal for his age. A low-grade temperature fits the viral trigger. The missed controller medicine is a risk factor that needs teaching, but it is not a sign of distress.

items.stem: The nurse notes diminished air movement at the lung bases. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: Airflow is severely limited; a quieter chest can mean the obstruction is getting worse
The wheezing is resolving because the airways are opening
It shows pneumonia with consolidation in both bases
It is a normal finding in children because of the thin chest wall
items.rationale: Wheezing needs moving air. When the airways narrow so much that little air moves, breath sounds and wheezes fade. A "quiet" or silent chest in a child who is still working hard to breathe is an ominous sign, not improvement. Consolidation would be focal with crackles or bronchial breath sounds, and a thin chest wall makes breath sounds louder, not softer.

items.stem: Complete the diagram: the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

opts: Give nebulized albuterol and ipratropium with oxygen
Lay the child flat to listen to the posterior lung fields
Give a sedative to ease his anxiety
Delay treatment until a peak flow reading is obtained
Work of breathing and air movement

items.rationale: A child with known asthma, a viral trigger, a missed controller and diffuse wheezing on both sides is having an asthma exacerbation. Foreign-body aspiration usually causes sudden, one-sided findings. Croup causes a barky cough and stridor in younger children. Anaphylaxis comes with hives or swelling after an exposure. A short-acting bronchodilator with ipratropium opens the airways, and an early systemic steroid treats the inflammation. Lying flat worsens breathing, sedatives can stop it, and a child this breathless cannot do a reliable peak flow. SpO₂ and work of breathing (retractions, speech, air entry) show whether treatment is working.

items.stem: At 09:10, after three albuterol–ipratropium treatments and oral dexamethasone, he still has severe retractions and an SpO₂ of 91% on 2 L. For each possible order, mark whether it is indicated or not indicated.
rows: Magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg IV over 20 minutes
items.rationale: When the first hour of treatment fails, IV magnesium relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, continuous albuterol keeps the airways open, and oxygen is raised to the target range. Chest physiotherapy and mucolytics do not help in an acute attack and can trigger more bronchospasm. Agitation in a hypoxic child is a sign of poor oxygenation; sedation can suppress breathing and lead to respiratory arrest.

items.stem: Magnesium was given at 09:15 and continuous albuterol is running. A venous blood gas at 10:00 shows pH 7.24 and PCO₂ 58 mm Hg. Review the trend. Which action should the nurse take first?

rows: Wheezes in and out, all fields

options: Call for immediate help from the provider and resuscitation team and prepare to assist breathing with a bag-valve mask on 100% oxygen
Document that the wheezing has resolved and space out the treatments
Let the child sleep because he is finally resting
Repeat the blood gas in 1 hour
items.rationale: A falling respiratory rate, a silent chest, worsening SpO₂ on more oxygen, drowsiness and a rising PCO₂ with acidosis show that the child is tiring and heading into respiratory failure. He needs immediate help with ventilation and the team for advanced airway support. The wheeze is gone because air is not moving, not because he is better. Drowsiness here comes from CO₂ retention, and waiting an hour could lead to arrest.

items.stem: Six hours after transfer to the pediatric ICU on high-flow nasal cannula and continuous albuterol: for each finding, mark whether the client has improved, not changed, or declined.
rows: Awake and asking for his tablet
Expiratory wheezes now heard in all fields
items.rationale: Better alertness, full sentences, a slower respiratory rate, less retraction and good SpO₂ on less oxygen show recovery. Hearing wheezes again after a silent chest means air is moving through the airways again, which is improvement. Frequent or continuous albuterol shifts potassium into the cells, so hypokalemia is a known side effect. Report it and expect replacement and cardiac monitoring.

title: Acute Ischemic Stroke
profile: 71-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes, brought by EMS at 10:20. His wife last saw him normal at 08:50 and found him at 09:30 slumped in his chair, unable to speak clearly. He takes no anticoagulants.

Notes: Right facial droop. Right arm drifts to the bed within 10 seconds; right leg drifts. Speaks only a few words and cannot name objects, but follows simple commands. Eyes deviate to the left. NIHSS 14. Weight 80 kg.
Vitals: BP 196/112 mm Hg · HR 108, irregularly irregular (new atrial fibrillation) · RR 18 · SpO₂ 95% on room air · T 36.9 °C (98.4 °F)
Labs: Platelets 228,000/µL · INR 1.0 · aPTT 29 seconds · Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL
Noncontrast CT head: no hemorrhage. CT angiography: occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery (M1).
Orders: Stroke alert · Labetalol 10 mg IV over 1–2 minutes; may repeat once for BP > 185/110 mm Hg · Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus (20 mg) once BP < 185/110 mm Hg · Interventional neuroradiology consult for thrombectomy · NPO until bedside swallow screen · Neuro checks and BP every 15 minutes × 2 hours, every 30 minutes × 6 hours, then hourly × 16 hours · Keep BP < 180/105 mm Hg for 24 hours after thrombolysis

items.stem: Which findings require immediate follow-up by the stroke team? Select all that apply.
options: Right arm drifts to the bed within 10 seconds
Speaks only a few words and cannot name objects
items.rationale: The last-known-well time decides treatment eligibility. A BP above 185/110 must be lowered before a thrombolytic. One-sided weakness and aphasia are deficits that are tracked closely for change. New atrial fibrillation is a likely source of the clot and needs follow-up. The glucose was checked to rule out hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic and is acceptable. Oxygen is not needed while SpO₂ stays at 94% or higher, and he has no fever.

items.stem: Complete the sentences.

blanks.pre: Right-sided weakness with trouble speaking points to a stroke in the
The window for IV thrombolysis is counted from
opts: 08:50, when he was last known well
10:20, when he arrived at the hospital
blanks.answer: 08:50, when he was last known well

items.rationale: Motor pathways cross, so a left-hemisphere stroke weakens the right side, and the language centers are in the left hemisphere in most people. The eyes look toward the side of the lesion. When onset is not witnessed, the clock starts at the last time the client was seen normal, not when symptoms were found or when he arrived: 08:50 plus 4.5 hours is 13:20.

items.stem: The CT shows no bleeding. Which finding must be corrected before a thrombolytic can be given?
options: Atrial fibrillation with a heart rate of 108
items.rationale: BP must be below 185/110 mm Hg before thrombolysis and kept below 180/105 mm Hg for 24 hours afterward, because high pressure raises the risk of bleeding into the brain. Atrial fibrillation is not a contraindication. Only a glucose below 50 mg/dL must be corrected first. There is no upper age limit for thrombolysis.

items.stem: Complete the diagram: the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

opts: Acute ischemic stroke from a large-vessel occlusion
Give IV labetalol to bring BP below 185/110 mm Hg
Give the tenecteplase bolus once BP is below 185/110 mm Hg
Give aspirin 325 mg by mouth now
Start a heparin infusion for the atrial fibrillation
Lower the BP quickly to 120/80 mm Hg
Capillary refill in the right hand

items.rationale: The CT shows no blood, the glucose is normal and the deficits are still present, while the CT angiogram shows a blocked M1 artery: an ischemic stroke from a large-vessel occlusion, not a TIA. Lowering the BP just enough makes him eligible, and tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg) is an accepted choice for IV thrombolysis. Because an M1 occlusion is a large-vessel occlusion, he should also go on to thrombectomy without waiting to see whether the thrombolytic works. Aspirin and heparin are not given within 24 hours of thrombolysis, and he is NPO until a swallow screen. Dropping the BP to normal reduces blood flow to the brain tissue that can still be saved. Neuro checks and BP are the key checks for bleeding and worsening stroke.

items.stem: Tenecteplase 20 mg IV was given at 11:00, and the client is waiting in the emergency department for the thrombectomy team. Review the flow sheet. At 12:00 the client reports a severe headache and has vomited once. Select all actions the nurse should take now.
options: Prepare the client for a STAT noncontrast CT of the head
Draw STAT CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen and type and crossmatch
Treat the BP per protocol to keep it below 180/105 mm Hg
Give aspirin 325 mg for the headache
Continue neuro checks on the routine hourly schedule
Give an antiemetic and reassess in 1 hour before calling
items.rationale: A new severe headache, vomiting, a BP surge and an NIHSS that jumps from 10 to 16 after thrombolysis mean brain hemorrhage until a CT proves otherwise. Notify the provider, get an emergency CT, send the labs needed to reverse a bleed, and bring the BP back under 180/105. Aspirin adds bleeding risk and is not given within 24 hours of thrombolysis. Neuro checks are due every 15 minutes in the first 2 hours, and any decline needs action now, not in 1 hour.

items.stem: The 12:05 CT showed no bleeding, and the client had a mechanical thrombectomy that reopened the artery. Twenty-four hours later: for each finding, mark whether the client has improved, not changed, or declined.
rows: Right arm lifts and holds for 10 seconds
Speaks in short sentences with some word-finding pauses
New firm, 6 cm swelling at the right groin puncture site
items.rationale: The lower NIHSS, stronger arm, better speech and a BP within the post-thrombolysis limit show a good response. The heart rhythm is unchanged, and he will need long-term stroke prevention for it, which the team will plan. A new firm swelling at the groin access site suggests a hematoma. Apply firm manual pressure just above the puncture site, check distal pulses and notify the provider; back or flank pain with falling BP would suggest a retroperitoneal bleed.
